[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Ruprecht_I_mit_Frauen.jpg/250px-Ruprecht_I_mit_Frauen.jpg)](/wiki/File:Ruprecht_I_mit_Frauen.jpg)

In 1386, Heidelberg University was founded by [Rupert I](/wiki/Rupert_I,_Elector_Palatine "Rupert I, Elector Palatine") on instruction of [Pope Urban VI](/wiki/Pope_Urban_VI "Pope Urban VI") who demanded modelling it after the ancient [University of Paris](/wiki/University_of_Paris "University of Paris").

The [Great Schism](/wiki/Western_Schism "Western Schism") of 1378 made it possible for Heidelberg, a relatively small city and capital of the [Electorate of the Palatinate](/wiki/Electorate_of_the_Palatinate "Electorate of the Palatinate"), to gain its own university.[[19]](#cite_note-Cser31-19) The Great Schism was initiated by the election of two popes after the death of [Pope Gregory XI](/wiki/Pope_Gregory_XI "Pope Gregory XI") in the same year.[[19]](#cite_note-Cser31-19) One successor resided in [Avignon](/wiki/Avignon "Avignon") (elected by the French) and the other in Rome (elected by the Italian cardinals).[[19]](#cite_note-Cser31-19) The German secular and spiritual leaders voiced their support for the successor in Rome, which had far-reaching consequences for the German students and teachers in Paris: they lost their stipends and had to leave.[[20]](#cite_note-20)

[Rupert I](/wiki/Rupert_I,_Elector_Palatine_of_the_Rhine "Rupert I, Elector Palatine of the Rhine") recognized the opportunity and initiated talks with the [Curia](/wiki/Roman_Curia "Roman Curia"), which ultimately led to a [papal bull](/wiki/Papal_bull "Papal bull") for foundation of a university. After having received, on 23 October 1385, permission from pope [Urban VI](/wiki/Urban_VI "Urban VI") to create a school of general studies ([Latin](/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): *studium generale*), the final decision to found the university was taken on 26 June 1386 at the beh

Bank of America :: part 04 :: chunk_0003
Both Bank of America and Merrill Lynch Wealth Management retain large market shares in their respective offerings. As of 2018, the [investment bank](/wiki/Investment_banking "Investment banking") was considered within the "[bulge bracket](/wiki/Bulge_bracket "Bulge bracket")" as the world's [third-largest investment bank](/wiki/List_of_investment_banks "List of investment banks").[[6]](#cite_note-6) Its wealth management unit manages $1.08 trillion in [assets under management](/wiki/Assets_under_management "Assets under management") (AUM) as the [second-largest wealth manager in the world](/wiki/Private_banking#Private_banking_rankings "Private banking"), after [UBS](/wiki/UBS "UBS").[[7]](#cite_note-7) In commercial banking, Bank of America has operations, but does not necessarily maintain retail branches in all 50 states of the United States, [Washington, D.C.](/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."), and over 40 other countries.[[8]](#cite_note-8) Its commercial banking footprint encapsulates 46 million consumer and small-business relationships at 4,600 banking centers and 16,000 [automated teller machines](/wiki/Automated_teller_machine "Automated teller machine") (ATMs).

The bank's large market share, business activities, and economic impact have led to numerous lawsuits and investigations regarding both mortgages and financial disclosures dating back to the [2008 financial crisis](/wiki/2008_financial_crisis "2008 financial crisis"). Its corporate practices of servicing the [middle class](/wiki/Middle_class "Middle class") and wider banking community have yielded a substantial market share since the early 20th century. As of August 2018, Bank of America has a $313.5 billion [market capitalization](/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization"), making it the [13th largest company in the world](/wiki/List_of_public_corporations_by_market_capitalization "List of public corporations by market capitalization"). fanoutqa_009603.x:
Neptune :: History :: Status :: chunk_0007
From its discovery in 1846 until the [discovery of Pluto](/wiki/Discovery_of_Pluto "Discovery of Pluto") in 1930, Neptune was the farthest known planet. When [Pluto](/wiki/Pluto "Pluto") was discovered, it was considered a planet, and Neptune thus became the second-farthest known planet, except for a 20-year period between 1979 and 1999 when Pluto's elliptical orbit brought it closer than Neptune to the Sun, making Neptune the ninth planet from the Sun during this period.[[67]](#cite_note-73)[[68]](#cite_note-74) The increasingly accurate estimations of Pluto's mass from ten times [that of Earth's](/wiki/Earth_mass "Earth mass") to far less than [that of the Moon](/wiki/Lunar_mass "Lunar mass")[[69]](#cite_note-75) and the discovery of the [Kuiper belt](/wiki/Kuiper_belt "Kuiper belt") in 1992 led many astronomers to debate whether Pluto should be considered a planet or as part of the Kuiper belt.[[70]](#cite_note-76)[[71]](#cite_note-77) In 2006, the [International Astronomical Union](/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union") [defined the word "planet"](/wiki/IAU_definition_of_planet "IAU definition of planet") for the first time, reclassifying Pluto as a "[dwarf planet](/wiki/Dwarf_planet "Dwarf planet")" and making Neptune once again the outermost-known planet in the Solar System.[[72]](#cite_note-78)

The [rings of Saturn](/wiki/Rings_of_Saturn "Rings of Saturn")

Several planets or dwarf planets in the Solar System (such as Neptune and Pluto) have orbital periods that are in [resonance](/wiki/Orbital_resonance "Orbital resonance") with each other or with smaller bodies. This is common in satellite systems (e.g. the resonance between Io, [Europa](/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)"), and Ganymede around Jupiter, or between Enceladus and Dione around Saturn). All except Mercury and Venus have [natural satellites](/wiki/Natural_satellite "Natural satellite"), often called "moons". Earth has one, Mars has two, and the giant planets have numerous moons in complex planetary-type systems. Except for Ceres and Sedna, all the consensus dwarf planets are known to have at least one moon as well. Many moons of the giant planets have features similar to those on the terrestrial planets and dwarf planets, and some have been studied as possible abodes of life (especially Europa and Enceladus).[[142]](#cite_note-Grasset2000-143)[[143]](#cite_note-Fortes2000-144)[[144]](#cite_note-145)[[145]](#cite_note-Taubner_et_al._2018-146)[[146]](#cite_note-Affholder_et_al._2021-147)

The four giant planets are orbited by [planetary rings](/wiki/Planetary_ring "Planetary ring") of varying size and complexity. The rings are composed primarily of dust or particulate matter, but can host tiny '[moonlets](/wiki/Rings_of_Saturn#Propeller_moonlets "Rings of Saturn")' whose gravity shapes and maintains their structure. The [1890 United States census](/wiki/1890_United_States_census "1890 United States census") showed a total population of 1,515,301, the foreign-born were 639,943 at 42%. The city did not trust the accuracy of the census so conducted an 1890 New York City Police census. This census revealed a population of 1,710,715.[[8]](#cite_note-8)
During the early 20th century, from 1900 to 1940, New York City's population was predominantly White, accounting for over 93% of the population, with the Black community constituting less than 3%. By the 1950s, the White population decreased to around 90%, while the Black population increased to nearly 10%. From 1970 to 1980, more pronounced shifts occurred, with the White population dropping to 60.72%, the Black population increasing to 25.23%, and a notable rise in the Hispanic/Latino population to 19.88%. The 1990s brought further diversification, with the White population falling to 44.66% by 2000, and growth in the Black, Asian, and Hispanic/Latino populations. The most recent decade from 2010 to 2020 saw a continued decrease in the White population to 34.09%, significant growth in the Asian population to 15.73%, stability in the Black population around 22-25%, and growth in the Hispanic/Latino community to 28.29%. The Other or Mixed category also grew to 28.11%. Throughout this period, New York City remained a hub for immigrants, with the foreign-born population peaking at 37.51% in 2010. Overall, these trends reflect the transformation of New York City into an increasingly multicultural metropolis, with a progressive decline in the White population and expanding representation of Black, Asian, Hispanic/Latino, and Other or Mixed groups.[[1]](#cite_note-nycrace-1)[[9]](#cite_note-9)
